title: Build a tested local FAQ assistant
requirements: Python 3.10 or newer, a terminal and a text editor. No packages, model download, cloud account, GPU or API key. Installation may require internet; all supplied exercises run offline afterward. Commands use python; use python3 on systems where that is the installed command. Work in a new practice folder, never a production project.

lessons.title: Prepare a folder and trace a program
lessons.time: 20–40 minutes plus Python installation if needed
lessons.objective: Run a saved Python file from the correct directory and explain input, processing and output.
lessons.concept: A terminal runs commands in a working directory. A file path identifies a file. Python executes the statements in a .py file; text inside quotes is data.
actions: Check python --version. If unavailable, install Python from python.org using the official instructions for your OS, reopen the terminal, and check again.
Create a folder named atlas-practice with your file manager. Open a terminal there (or use cd followed by its full path). Keep every workshop file in this folder.
Save hello.py containing the three lines below. Run python hello.py. Change the name, predict the output, and run again.

Optional Git extension: after installing Git, run git init, git add hello.py, and git commit -m "First program". Configure your preferred Git identity if Git requests it; Git is not needed to continue the core workshop.
lessons.expected: Hello, Learner before the edit. Your changed name should appear after the edit.
lessons.verify: Close and reopen the terminal, return to atlas-practice, and reproduce the output. Explain which line supplies input, which transforms it and which displays it.
lessons.troubleshoot: If Python cannot open the file, check the working directory and ensure the editor did not save hello.py.txt. If python is unavailable, try python3 or py -3 and use that command consistently.
lessons.challenge: Add a second variable for a topic and print a sentence containing both variables. Predict what happens if you remove one closing quote before trying it.
lessons.recall: Without copying, explain a command, a directory and a file path.
lessons.pass: Two reproducible runs with different input, plus an explanation of a syntax error and its correction.

lessons.title: Separate a decision from its interface
lessons.objective: Write and test a function with a defined input/output contract.
lessons.concept: A function receives input and returns a value. Returning a value lets a command-line client, a test and an HTTP service reuse the same logic. A deterministic rule produces the same result for the same input.
actions: Save the example as rules.py. Run python rules.py.
Explain strip(), casefold(), return and the equality comparison using the example.
Add assertions for HOURS, an unknown question and an empty string. Run the file again.
Change one expected result deliberately, observe the assertion failure, then correct it.
lessons.code:
def reply(question):
    if question.strip().casefold() == 'hours':
        return 'Open 09:00–17:00.'
    return 'Not found.'

assert reply(' hours ') == 'Open 09:00–17:00.'
assert reply('weather') == 'Not found.'
print('Rule checks passed')
lessons.expected: Rule checks passed when all assertions are correct; AssertionError when your deliberately incorrect expectation is used.
lessons.verify: Identify the recognized input, normalization, answer and fallback. Show that a failed expectation produces a visible error.
lessons.troubleshoot: Indent the function body consistently with four spaces. A missing colon or mixed indentation is a syntax issue; a wrong returned answer is a behavior issue.
lessons.challenge: Support location as a second question while keeping the original assertions passing. Decide how an empty question should be handled.
lessons.recall: Explain why return is useful even when nothing is printed.
lessons.pass: Original and new question checks pass, unknown input has an explicit fallback, and the learner explains the rule without reading a prepared answer.

lessons.title: Inspect and test a tiny dataset
lessons.objective: Measure missing fields and exact duplicate records before choosing a cleaning policy.
lessons.concept: Missing data is not zero. An exact duplicate row differs from a repeated identifier containing conflicting values. Profiling measures the issue; cleaning requires a stated policy.
actions: Copy customers.csv, inspect_data.py and test_data.py from the reference files below into atlas-practice.
Run python inspect_data.py and compare each count with the four CSV records manually.
Run python -m unittest test_data -v. Keep the original fixture unchanged while experimenting in a second CSV file.

Write a cleaning policy: retain one copy of an exact duplicate, preserve missing ages as unknown, and reject conflicting records with the same customer_id for manual review. Explain why a missing age must not become zero automatically.
lessons.expected: 4 rows; 3 columns; missing customer_id=0, age=2, city=1; 1 excess exact duplicate row. The two supplied data tests pass.
lessons.verify: Manually recount after editing your separate fixture. Distinguish the raw count from any cleaned count and record which file each result describes.
lessons.troubleshoot: Use UTF-8 and a comma-separated file. If you see a single column, inspect the delimiter. Never overwrite the raw fixture to hide a failed assertion.
lessons.challenge: Implement the cleaning policy in a new function. Add a fifth record with customer_id=2 and a different city; prove that it is flagged instead of silently dropped.
lessons.recall: Revisit Lesson 2: which parts should be functions so they can be tested without printing?
lessons.pass: Correct raw counts, a justified policy, and an independent conflicting-record example with a test. The profiler alone does not complete the cleaning challenge.
hints: Start with a list of row dictionaries. Keep a dictionary whose key is customer_id and value is a list of distinct versions.
Skip an exact duplicate dictionary. If an ID has two different dictionaries, quarantine every version instead of silently keeping the first.
Compare a missing-age record with an identical copy, then a record with the same ID and a different city. Preserve the empty age.

lessons.title: Decide whether a model is needed
lessons.objective: Compare exact rules with a proposed model using an explicit quality and cost decision.
lessons.concept: This workshop's assistant uses exact rules, not machine learning or an LLM. Models may handle language variation but introduce uncertainty, latency, cost and data-handling questions. A plausible answer can still be unsupported.
actions: Create evaluation.csv with columns question,expected_answer,split. Example: hours,Open 09:00–17:00.,development. Write at least six development cases and have a peer prepare four held-out cases when possible. Otherwise reserve four cases without using them to edit the rule. Cover recognized, unknown, blank, case/space variation and paraphrases.
Run the rules from Lesson 2 on development cases. Record correct answers, explicit abstentions and unsupported answers separately.
Write a design decision comparing rules, keyword retrieval and an optional hosted model. State when the rules are sufficient and what evidence would justify a model.

For an offline model comparison, label a few saved hypothetical outputs as correct, unsupported or uncertain. Label them simulated; do not report measured model cost or performance without an actual run.
lessons.expected: A small evaluation table and a decision that distinguishes measured rule behavior from proposed or simulated model behavior.
lessons.verify: Keep the held-out cases unused while editing the rule. Report the numerator and denominator of every rate; a tiny fixture is not a reliable estimate of deployment quality.
lessons.troubleshoot: If a model sounds convincing, check whether the answer is supported by an allowed source. A source ID alone does not establish that the content supports the claim.
lessons.challenge: Add the paraphrase 'When do you open?' to development cases. Improve the rule using development cases only. Keep held-out cases unused until Lesson 7; once inspected, treat them as consumed and create new held-out cases for another independent evaluation.
lessons.recall: Explain why duplicate data and tuning on evaluation examples can make apparent quality misleading.
lessons.pass: A justified baseline decision, separate development/held-out cases, and an honest account of measured versus simulated evidence.

lessons.title: Expose a local request contract
lessons.objective: Send JSON to a local service and handle rejected requests and service failure.
lessons.concept: HTTP carries a request and response. JSON is a data format. A service must validate the request; syntactically valid JSON does not establish valid business input. Keep reusable logic separate from transport.
actions: Copy assistant.py, client.py and test_assistant.py from the reference files below. Read answer() before examining the HTTP handler.
In terminal A, run python assistant.py. In terminal B, from atlas-practice, run python client.py.
Inspect the /ask route, Content-Type, response status and the response fields answer and source. Change the client's question to project and explain the guest fallback.
Stop terminal A with Ctrl+C and rerun the client. It must show service unavailability rather than an invented response. Restart the service if you want another manual request.
lessons.expected: The hours request returns source public-hours. The guest project request returns no source. With the server stopped, the client prints the service-unavailable recovery message.
lessons.verify: Run python -m unittest test_assistant.EndpointTests -v. The tests start their own temporary local server; the manual server need not be running.
lessons.troubleshoot: If port 8765 is busy, stop your previous workshop process. If you choose another port, change both the server and client. A 400 response is a rejected input; a connection error means there was no usable service response.
lessons.challenge: Add a request example containing a JSON list rather than an object and confirm a 400 response. Explain why the client must not retry every 400 indefinitely.
lessons.recall: Which Lesson 2 function boundary lets you test answers without starting a server?
lessons.pass: Valid request, invalid request and unavailable-service behavior are reproduced and explained.

lessons.title: Keep identity and source permissions separate
lessons.objective: Demonstrate user isolation and explain why untrusted input cannot grant access.
lessons.concept: Authorization decides which records an identity can access. The toy HTTP service fixes the identity to guest; it has no login system. The internal answer() user argument represents an already trusted caller. A real service must derive identity from verified authentication, not a JSON user field.
actions: Run python -m unittest test_assistant.AnswerTests -v and inspect the permission and deletion tests.
Trace permitted records for alice, bob and guest. Explain why filtering happens before selecting an answer.
Inspect test_request_cannot_choose_identity: a request claiming user=alice must still act as guest.
Draw or describe the boundaries between request data, trusted identity, stored source content and returned output. Use synthetic records only.
lessons.expected: Alice and Bob receive their own project records; guest receives neither. Deleted records are unavailable. Instruction-like text does not grant permission.
lessons.verify: Show the record IDs permitted for each identity. Explain why the exact-match fixture's instruction test does not establish that an LLM application is resistant to prompt injection.
lessons.troubleshoot: If a request body selects its own identity, remove that behavior. If you add real authentication later, validate identity at the boundary and test failures before accepting it.
lessons.challenge: Add a second synthetic Alice-only record and a cross-user test. Then remove that record and prove the old answer cannot be retrieved.
lessons.recall: Revisit the baseline decision: what new trust boundary appears if a third-party model receives context?
lessons.pass: Positive and negative permission tests, deletion behavior, and an explanation of the trusted-caller assumption.

lessons.title: Review evidence and catch a regression
lessons.objective: Distinguish regression checks from evidence of general quality and demonstrate a failed check.
lessons.concept: A test checks a property under specified conditions. Passing fixtures do not establish broad reliability, and self-reported completion is not independent verification.
actions: Run python -m unittest discover -v from atlas-practice. Save your actual output with Python version and the date.
Copy the project to a separate experiment folder. Deliberately change the public hours answer there, run the tests, and identify the failing expectation. Restore the correct behavior and rerun.
Review the held-out questions from Lesson 4 once. Record answer quality, abstention and unsupported claims without changing the system based on those same cases and claiming an independent score.
Write an evaluation note with observed failures, untested conditions, sample size and the limitations of a deterministic fixture.
lessons.expected: All supplied tests pass on the reference files. If you completed the optional cleaning reference extension, include its tests too. Your deliberate regression fails a relevant test; restoring it returns the suite to passing.
lessons.verify: Explain what each test family establishes and one failure it cannot detect. Keep both failed and passing transcripts.
lessons.troubleshoot: If no tests are found, check that filenames begin test_ and the terminal is in atlas-practice. If a networking test fails because local sockets are restricted, record that limitation and run the pure function and data tests separately.
lessons.challenge: Add an oversized question and a malformed JSON request test without copying a solution. Explain the expected HTTP behavior before running it.
lessons.recall: Explain the difference between a reproducible regression suite and an estimate of real user quality.
lessons.pass: A demonstrated regression, recovery, an independently added negative case and an evaluation note that does not overstate the evidence.

lessons.title: Adapt, explain and hand over the project
lessons.objective: Independently change a small service and give someone enough evidence to reproduce it.
lessons.concept: Working knowledge includes adapting the system, diagnosing a failure and explaining limitations. A local fixture exercises engineering skills but does not demonstrate LLM training, production authentication or operational readiness.
actions: Without opening the sample extension below, add a public location record and tests for normalized input, an unknown question and source attribution. Preserve all existing behavior.
Write README.md with Python version, exact startup/test commands, three request scenarios, the identity assumption, data policy and known limitations.
Recreate the project in a fresh folder using your handover instructions and run every test.
Record a short review answering: why these rules, why these permission boundaries, what fails without the server, and what would change before using real user data or an actual model?
lessons.expected: A repeatable local project, all original tests plus your new tests, and evidence of one diagnosed failure and its correction.
lessons.verify: Use the assessment rubric below. Ask a peer or tutor to select an unfamiliar input and a small change request. If no reviewer is available, label the assessment self-reviewed.
lessons.troubleshoot: If fresh-folder setup fails, correct the handover instructions and rerun from the beginning. Do not copy hidden environment dependencies into an unexplained setup.
lessons.challenge: Add a second permitted public question with an answer that differs only in punctuation. Keep response semantics separate from formatting and explain your test choice.
lessons.recall: After two days, explain the architecture without the code. After one week, repeat one permission test and one change request before reviewing your notes.
lessons.pass: A clean-folder run, independently added behavior and tests, an explained failure, accurate limitations, and all four rubric dimensions passing.
